name: Private Eye Cyclops crossword No 589
preamble: Running clockwise around the shaded squares, starting top left, are two sentences from a 2016 ‘Pseuds Corner’ entry. Cuts have been made to fit the quote in the grid. One clue, lacking a definition, leads to the perpetrator’s name. The 52 letters of the quote not intersecting with clue answers are: AAAAAA EEEEE FF H IIIIII K LLL M N OOOOOO PPP RRRR SS TTTTTT U WWW Y

solutions.check: 66 entries verified against the grid image (lengths, crossings, linked-clue mapping); unclued letters checked against the preamble's list

clue.text: Cyclops’ attitude on having an erection and performing? “Burden”

blocks.note: the setter is Cyclops, so 'Cyclops' is' becomes 'I am', shortened to I'M
a pose is a stance or attitude
standing up, in the crude Private Eye sense
an actor who is performing is on

explanation.surface: A smutty question about the setter's stance when aroused and on stage, followed by a one-word verdict.
explanation.walkthrough: The setter's pen name stands for the first person here, so the possessive-looking opening is really 'I am'.
explanation.definitionFit: To impose upon someone is to put a load or demand on them, exactly as a verb meaning to burden does.

clue.text: Raving about ill-judged war, one takes on Cameron, primarily

indicators.note: to come about is to turn round, so the letters face the other way
primarily means first of all, so only the opening letter of the word counts

blocks.note: 'Nam is the Vietnam War, widely seen as a misjudged war
the initial of Cameron, then the Prime Minister

explanation.surface: Someone rants about a disastrous war while one person goes head to head with David Cameron.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Nam is American slang for Vietnam and its war; reversed, it opens the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Raving and manic both describe wild, frenzied, excessively excited behaviour bordering on madness.

clue.text: Constable’s work possibly is about protecting suspect Sun – clear?

indicators.note: a suspect account is unreliable, so the letters cannot be trusted in this order
to protect is to surround and shield, so one piece wraps around the rest

explanation.surface: A police constable's job is to shield a suspect from the Sun newspaper, and the clue asks if that is plain.
explanation.walkthrough: Constable is not a police officer but John Constable, the English painter of landscapes such as The Hay Wain; the Sun is a British tabloid.
explanation.definitionFit: John Constable painted countryside views, so a typical canvas of his is an example of a countryside picture.

clue.text: Exaggerate what Archer was given

blocks.note: second meaning: British slang for a prison sentence, which the novelist Jeffrey Archer served for perjury

explanation.walkthrough: Jeffrey Archer, novelist and Conservative peer, was jailed in 2001 for perjury; in British slang a spell in prison is a stretch.
explanation.definitionFit: To stretch a story is to overstate it, and a term served inside jail is also called by this slang noun.

clue.text: ‘Fizzy‘ Philip gets into Fanny’s skirts

indicators.note: getting into something means going inside it, so one piece sits within another
skirts are the outer edges of something, so only the outside letters are kept

blocks.note: the first and last letters of Fanny

explanation.surface: A lively man called Philip slips under a woman's skirts, in classic Private Eye innuendo.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fizzy' is set apart as a nickname, but it is the definition; Philip is the writer Philip Roth.
explanation.definitionFit: Fizzy drinks have a head of bubbles, so effervescent and foam-topped liquids can be called by either word.

clue.text: Accepting Labour’s leader is in struggle and making yourself scarce

indicators.note: a leader goes in front, so just the first letter is wanted
being in something means sitting inside it, so one piece goes within another

explanation.surface: The Labour leader is caught up in an internal battle while quietly trying to slip away.
explanation.walkthrough: In 2016 Jeremy Corbyn faced a leadership challenge, which gives the surface its bite.
explanation.definitionFit: Running away or fleeing is a common idiomatic sense, so disappearing quickly from a place fits both phrases.

clue.text: Republicans’ heart cuts support – support that’s common in N. America

definitions.note: a descriptive clause for a noun: the answer is an animal widespread in North America

indicators.note: the heart is the centre, so only the middle letter is kept
to cut into something is to go inside it, so one piece sits within another

blocks.note: the central letter of the eleven in Republicans
to back someone is to support them
to bear a weight is to support it

explanation.surface: American politics: a core of Republicans undercuts support for something that is the norm across North America.
explanation.walkthrough: The repeated 'support' is used twice in two different senses, and the end of the clue only hints at an animal that is widespread there.
explanation.definitionFit: This dark-furred species is the most numerous ursine animal across Canada and the United States, so it is widespread there.

clue.text: Like a communist embraced by old Northerner – divine!

indicators.note: something embraced is held in the arms, so one piece sits inside the other

blocks.note: the Picts were an ancient people of northern Scotland

explanation.surface: A red is hugged by an old northerner, with an exclamation that it is heavenly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'divine!' reads as an exclamation of delight, but it is the verb meaning to foresee.
explanation.definitionFit: To divine the future is to foretell it by insight, so the verb shares the sense of forecasting what will happen.

clue.text: Line taken by PM once at special ace place for constitutional revival

indicators.note: something taken by another is captured and held inside it

blocks.note: L is the abbreviation for line
SP is an abbreviation for special
A is the card abbreviation for ace

explanation.surface: A former Prime Minister draws a line at a special place for reviving the constitution.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Constitutional' suggests politics, but here it means one's bodily make-up, as in a strong constitution.
explanation.definitionFit: A resort offering treatments and exercise restores bodily wellbeing, which is what your physical constitution means.

clue.text: Catch drugs, reportedly for the use of swinging entertainer

definitions.text: for the use of swinging entertainer
definitions.note: a descriptive phrase for a noun: the apparatus an acrobat swings on

indicators.note: what is reported is passed on by word of mouth, so go by sound rather than spelling

blocks.note: Es are ecstasy tablets; said as a word the plural sounds like these letters

explanation.surface: A drugs bust is reported as being aimed at a swinging entertainer, swinging in the 1960s party sense.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Swinging' suggests a louche lifestyle, but the entertainer here literally swings, high above the circus ring.
explanation.definitionFit: A circus acrobat performs on a horizontal bar hung from ropes, so the apparatus is used by an aerial performer.

clue.text: Make an MP of Tim? Well, at heart, that’s shocking

indicators.note: the heart is the centre, so only the middle letters are kept

blocks.note: voters elect a Member of Parliament
the two central letters of the word

explanation.surface: Someone asks whether to put a man called Tim into Parliament and is told that would be scandalous.
explanation.walkthrough: Tim needs his surname: Tim Rice wrote the lyrics for Evita and Jesus Christ Superstar. 'Shocking' means scandalous on the surface but literally delivers a jolt.
explanation.definitionFit: This fish stuns prey with a powerful discharge of current, so it is literally a creature that gives jolts.

clue.text: Take possession of Vine broadcast after a short while

indicators.note: to broadcast seed is to scatter it, so the letters are scattered into a new order

blocks.note: a mo is a moment, as in 'just a mo'

explanation.surface: Jeremy Vine, the BBC broadcaster, takes over something soon after going on air.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Broadcast' suggests Jeremy Vine's radio show, which makes it look like a sound clue; here it means scattered.
explanation.definitionFit: To occupy a new home you settle into it, which is how you assume ownership or occupancy of a property.

clue.text: Luvvies who went about telling sorry pals to get stuffed

indicators.note: being told to get stuffed is a rude dismissal; the letters are roughly dismissed from their order

explanation.surface: Pompous actors go round telling their sad friends to get lost.
explanation.walkthrough: Luvvies is British slang, slightly mocking, for actors and theatre people, from their habit of calling everyone 'luvvie'.
explanation.definitionFit: Touring actors of old travelled from town to town performing, so theatricals who toured around are exactly this.

clue.text: Sun separates Virgin and celebrity – that’s reportable!

indicators.note: something that separates two things comes between them, so it sits inside

blocks.note: virgin means unused or new, as in virgin snow
S is the abbreviation for Sun, as in Sunday
a worthy is a notable or eminent person

explanation.surface: The Sun tabloid gets between Virgin boss Richard Branson and a celebrity, which makes a story.
explanation.walkthrough: Sun and Virgin both look like company names, but they are an abbreviation and a plain adjective.
explanation.definitionFit: Something worth putting in the papers is significant enough for journalists to cover, as both phrases say.

clue.text: “One who thinks about an heir” – Brenda

blocks.note: a son is a typical heir
Brenda is Private Eye's nickname for the Queen, Elizabeth Regina

explanation.surface: A quotation attributed to the Queen about someone brooding over the succession.
explanation.walkthrough: Private Eye has long called Queen Elizabeth II 'Brenda', and ER is her royal cipher.
explanation.definitionFit: A person who uses logic and argument to reach conclusions is one who thinks things through carefully.

clue.text: May’s opening dig is due, about “not having proper leadership”

indicators.note: an opening is the very start, so just the first letter is used
turned about means moved around, so these letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: Theresa May's first jibe is overdue, aimed at a party lacking proper leadership.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is read playfully: to be badly guided is to lack proper direction from those in charge.
explanation.definitionFit: Misguided normally means wrongheaded, but literally it is being steered wrongly by those in charge, a punning reading.

clue.text: Not showing yourself to be Archer-like: vulgar

blocks.note: Jeffrey Archer was jailed for perjury, that is for lying

explanation.surface: Behaving like Jeffrey Archer is coarse, the clue says, unless you keep your head down.
explanation.walkthrough: Jeffrey Archer, novelist and Tory peer, was convicted of perjury in 2001; the setter returns to him from 15 across.
explanation.definitionFit: To stay out of sight and avoid attention is the idiomatic meaning, like an animal crouching hidden.

clue.text: Nick ‘Ace’ Clegg, primarily advanced to be a viral victim

indicators.note: primarily means first of all, so only the initial letter counts

blocks.note: to nick a thief is to catch one
A is the card abbreviation for ace

explanation.surface: Former Lib Dem leader Nick Clegg, nicknamed 'Ace', is promoted to become the victim of a viral attack.
explanation.walkthrough: Nick Clegg's first name is not a name at all: nick is British slang for arrest.
explanation.definitionFit: Being infected by the common rhinovirus makes you a casualty of a germ, which is what the phrase describes.

clue.text: Blow being in an unenlightened state!

definitions.text: Blow being in an unenlightened state

blocks.note: to blow a tune through pursed lips
without light, and also ignorant of the facts

explanation.surface: Someone blunders out of sheer ignorance.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Blow' looks like a punch or a mistake; read literally, the whole clue describes making a tune while sitting without light, which is also the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom means putting on a show of bravery or confidence that you do not feel, as a frightened walker might at night.

clue.text: Mean to get Donald finally locked up

indicators.note: finally means at the end, so only the last letter is kept

blocks.note: close means stingy, as in close-fisted

explanation.surface: Someone intends to see Donald Trump finally put behind bars.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Mean' reads as 'intend', but it is the adjective for tight with money.
explanation.definitionFit: A building that is shut and secured for the night with its doors bolted is both of these things.

clue.text: Who’d protect England from Boris, ultimately isn’t casual Osborne!

indicators.note: ultimately means in the end, so only the final letter is kept

blocks.note: ain't is the casual, slangy form of isn't
George Osborne, then Chancellor of the Exchequer

explanation.surface: Someone asks who will protect England from Boris Johnson, and concludes it is not the laid-back George Osborne.
explanation.walkthrough: 'casual' looks like a description of Osborne, but it turns 'isn't' into its informal version.
explanation.definitionFit: The patron saint of England, the dragon-slayer on its flag, is traditionally the nation's heavenly protector.

clue.text: Mate, getting on runner?

blocks.note: a runner bean is a climbing garden bean

explanation.surface: Someone asks whether their friend is still fit enough to be a runner.
explanation.walkthrough: A runner is not an athlete but the runner bean, a climbing vegetable common in British gardens.
explanation.definitionFit: This dated upper-class British form of address for a friend means the same as chum or pal.

clue.text: Clinton approaching: senior leaders very cautious – that won’t fly

indicators.note: leaders go at the front, so only the first letter of each word is taken

blocks.note: the initials of the three words
so means very, as in so tired

explanation.surface: As Hillary Clinton nears power, senior figures are wary: her plan will not take off.
explanation.walkthrough: 'that won't fly' sounds like a dismissed idea, but it is literal: this big Australasian bird is flightless.
explanation.definitionFit: This large Australasian bird is flightless like the emu, so it literally cannot take to the air.

clue.text: America taking Donald’s lead in ultimately psychotic, unfair and bizarre campaign

indicators.note: the lead is the front position, so only the first letter is kept
ultimately means in the end, so the final letter of each word is kept
in places one piece inside the frame formed by the others

blocks.note: the last letters of the two words

explanation.surface: America follows Donald Trump into a psychotic, unfair and bizarre election campaign.
explanation.walkthrough: The ends of the three adjectives make a frame; 'and' between the last two simply joins them.
explanation.definitionFit: A crusade is a vigorous organised drive for a cause, the same sense as a political or moral campaign.

clue.text: Endured dodgy President, North having conceded to South

indicators.note: conceding means giving way to a rival, so one letter yields its place to another
something dodgy is unsound, so these letters are not in a reliable order

blocks.note: N is the compass abbreviation; it is the letter replaced
S is the compass abbreviation, the letter brought in

explanation.surface: Voters put up with a shady President after the North lost out to the South.
explanation.walkthrough: The N of the word is swapped for S before the letters are rearranged.
explanation.definitionFit: To keep going in spite of difficulty is to carry on and hold out, both senses of the past-tense verb.

clue.text: see 62ac.
Dawn‘s about to finish bonking?

definitions.note: a clause: 'dawn's coming' means it is about to arrive
a verb phrase; the answer is its present participle

blocks.note: first meaning: approaching, as daybreak does
second meaning: reaching orgasm, in slang

explanation.surface: A woman named Dawn is almost done in bed.

clue.text: Sexually ready as a man?

clue.text: Treated for injury, being a victim of corrupt cops?

blocks.clueFragment: being a victim of corrupt cops

explanation.walkthrough: In British slang to stitch someone up is to frame them for something they did not do.

clue.text: ‘Earth-mover’ Boris’s last to leave house of ill repute

explanation.surface: Boris Johnson, the great earth-mover, has finally to leave a brothel.

clue.text: Literary response to doctor – unlikely to be said by Corbyn to his deputy on how their differences could be resolved?

blocks.note: second meaning: Corbyn's deputy was Tom Watson, and their quarrels were far from simple to settle

explanation.walkthrough: In 2016 Labour's deputy leader was Tom Watson, often at odds with Jeremy Corbyn; telling him a fix was obvious would be wildly optimistic.

clue.text: Innocent member breaks ice perhaps with Lib Dem has-been?

indicators.note: perhaps signals one possible version, so the letters may come in another order
to break into something is to get inside it

blocks.note: Vince Cable, the Liberal Democrat minister who lost his seat in 2015

clue.text: Disney mania, mismanaged balls up

explanation.walkthrough: Disney is not the company but Walt Disney himself, an example of the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Walt Disney made cartoon films, drawing figures that move, so he is an instance of such a filmmaker.

clue.text: Mean to have crappy climax underneath pop star

clue.text: Overwhelming acts of Scottish cack assembly

clue.text: Well, well Corbyn! EU’s upset with Anne hogging energy

clue.text: Measure May, ultimately, in bizarre bluff – “F-off, that’s more than enough!”

clue.text: Bank overdrawn, EU collapses (with a shove) – crack up

clue.text: Horny beast, absurdly macho, joins terrorists

clue.text: Hesitate to eject one from royal house

clue.text: No matter what’s stuck into fat that hangs from the neck

clue.text: Nuts-free city

blocks.note: rid means free, as in rid of

explanation.walkthrough: 'Nuts-free' looks like a food label, but the hyphen hides two separate pieces.

clue.text: Nike’s dodge, renovated seconds?

S, the initial of sex, plus core, meaning essence

explanation.surface: Seeking revenge, the President's wife sprays on a new sex-scented perfume.
explanation.walkthrough: 'First Lady' looks like a President's wife, but it is Eve, the first woman; to score is also slang for having sex, which suits the surface.
explanation.definitionFit: Settling an old grudge by paying someone back is to square things up, which this phrase means.

clue.text: “Acts like Pinochet regime,” papers said, recklessly

indicators.note: acting recklessly means without care, so the letters are thrown about carelessly

explanation.surface: Newspapers rashly report that someone behaves like General Pinochet's Chilean dictatorship.
explanation.walkthrough: Pinochet's regime in Chile abducted and secretly killed opponents, who became known as the disappeared; the verb is used transitively.
explanation.definitionFit: Under Pinochet thousands of dissidents were abducted and never seen again, so the regime made people vanish.

clue.text: Town‘s dispute about obsession

indicators.note: turned about means facing the other way

blocks.note: to have a thing about something is to be obsessed with it

explanation.surface: A town's quarrel over some fixation.
explanation.walkthrough: Worthing is a seaside town in West Sussex, England.
explanation.definitionFit: Worthing is a coastal resort on the English south coast, an example of a British town.

clue.text: Lib Dem humbled beside TV presenter

indicators.note: humbled means brought low and knocked about, so the letters are knocked into a new order

blocks.note: by means beside, as in sitting by the fire

explanation.surface: A Liberal Democrat is put in their place next to a television host.
explanation.walkthrough: David Dimbleby long chaired the BBC political debate show Question Time, where politicians are often humbled.
explanation.definitionFit: David and Jonathan Dimbleby are veteran BBC broadcasters who host political programmes on television.

clue.text: Green: a life ruined, without direction

indicators.note: something ruined is wrecked, so the letters are wrecked and rebuilt
without in its old sense means outside, so these letters go around another

explanation.walkthrough: 'without' looks like 'lacking', but it is the old sense of outside, so the shuffled letters wrap round the compass point.
explanation.definitionFit: A tree in leaf has its foliage out, so in spring it looks verdant, which is what the adjective means.

clue.text: Hot from female-only Private Eye occasion

indicators.note: taking one thing from another removes it

blocks.note: H for hot, as on a tap

explanation.surface: Hot news from a women-only Private Eye event.
explanation.walkthrough: Private Eye is the satirical magazine running this puzzle; here it is a private detective, who follows or tails suspects.
explanation.definitionFit: To entail is to involve or bring about as a consequence, which is the verb sense of occasion.

clue.text: Pass water: just a drop, darlin’

blocks.note: a sip is a tiny drink
hon, short for honey, is an endearment like darling

explanation.surface: Someone needing to urinate is told to manage only a dribble, darling.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pass water' means urinate on the surface but here means draw liquid through a tube; the clipped 'darlin'' hints the endearment is shortened too.
explanation.definitionFit: To siphon is to draw liquid from one container to another through a tube, moving it across.

clue.text: Financial institutions covering up a very sizeable depression

V is the abbreviation for very

explanation.walkthrough: 'depression' suggests an economic slump, which fits the banks; here it is a physical hollow.
explanation.definitionFit: A cavity is a hollow space or hole, a sunken area or dip of some size.

clue.text: Open crotch, twangy elasticated tights tops for players …

blocks.note: the first letters of the five words

explanation.walkthrough: 'players' suggests actors or the bedroom, but it is musicians; the ellipsis carries the joke into the next clue.
explanation.definitionFit: An octet is a group of eight musicians, so it is a band of players performing together.

clue.text: … which give briefs much support

blocks.note: surface reading: following the tights, things that hold up underpants
setter's reading: briefs are barristers, and the fees paid in court keep them in business

explanation.surface: The tights of the previous clue give good support to underwear.
explanation.walkthrough: A brief is British slang for a barrister or lawyer; the fees in litigation sustain them handsomely.
explanation.definitionFit: Fees and expenses paid in litigation fund the barristers and solicitors who handle a case, keeping them well paid.
